raw_comment:
Headline: Corona Light

I noticed that the coronavirus doesn't seem nearly as frightening, especially when compared to the extreme fatality rate of the bird flu, and the number of people affected by the measles. It’s fatality rate is between 0.1 and 5% and around 2 or 3 people infected by each sick person, while certainly serious, it is not as extreme when compared to other epidemics in the past. This is why I am so confused as to how the coronavirus is spreading so fast and so violently. In those first days, it practically doubled at the beginning, and even now it has around 82,000 total cases and 2,800 deaths. I don’t really understand how a disease that doesn't seem very serious when looking at this graph can have such an effect on our world currently. I mean something we should be more worried about is apparently the return of smallpox.

I wonder why the coronavirus is a box instead of a point. Where will the point be located when it becomes a point?

raw_comment: This graph shows how infectious certain diseases are and the mortality rates of these diseases, including coronavirus. Diseases graphed higher up have a greater mortality rate and diseases graphed farther right are more infectious. The graph shows diseases like the bird flu, ebola, and MERS to be highly fatal and the common cold and the chickenpox to be relatively harmless. It also shows MERS, the bird flu, and the seasonal flu to be uninfectious, but the chickenpox and measles to be very infectious. The graph represents the data for coronavirus in a red box, as there is probably not enough data to condense the disease into a single point. The fatality rate for coronavirus is between .1% and around 5%, and each sick person infects between 1 and 3 people. I wonder when scientists will have enough data to label coronavirus in a more accurate manner, and how many people total were infected by each disease. One possible title for this graph could be "Statistics on Infectious Diseases."

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph compares how deadly the most infectious diseases may be.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph and the map. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released in two days – Friday, Feb. 28 with moderation on Wednesday, March 4.  The topic – voter opinion polls.  The day after Super Tuesday.  Stay tuned.

raw_comment:
Noticing: I notice that measles can affect up to 15 people, yet it's fatality rate is less than 1%. Lower on the graph, I notice that the common cold and chickenpox have a fatality rate of 0%, but common cold can be spread to roughly 2 people, while chickenpox can spread to 8. On top of the graph, I see that bird flu has the highest fatality rate, at ~60 percent, but can only be spread to at least 1 person. The disease on this graph that is least likely for you to be infected is MERS. More recently, I notice that the corona virus has a range between 0.1% fatality rate to 4 percent. 

Wondering: I wonder why coronavirus has a range. Is it because it is still a developing virus? In addition to that why does measles have such a low fatality rate even though it spreads to more than a dozen people?

Title: Coronavirus and it's comparison to other diseases

3) This graph is showing the most common infectious diseases, comparing them to the new coronavirus by fatality rate and the average number of people infected by those who have it. A name for the graph could be “The Truth About the New Coronavirus...How Fatal is it Really?”

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice when I look at the graph is the fatality rate of the bird flu. While I have heard of this infectious disease, I haven’t seen as much media coverage about this sickness as I have the coronavirus. Additionally, I noticed that the measles are an outlier, sitting at about 15 people on average who are infected by each sick person, while the bird flu is much less. 

When looking at this graph and the different infectious diseases that can be spread amongst the population, I wonder why the coronavirus has caught the attention of the media to the extent in which it has, and why other diseases are being discussed about just as much or more. I also wonder how the development of these sicknesses will change the future of medicine and if there have been any revolutionary treatments that are in the works as of now, especially for the bird flu. 

If I had to title the graph to capture the fatality rate and average number of people infected by each person for these various diseases, I would title it: “The Dangerous Range of Disease.”

raw_comment:
I noticed the highest fatality rate belonged to the Bird Flu, however it was also one of the lowest infection rates. While Measles and Chickenpox were on the top for infection rates. Moreover, I noticed the Coronavirus had a large variability in death range from .1% to 5%. 

I wonder how new advancements in curative technology will impact the infection and fatality rate for the Coronavirus. Furthermore, what impacts it will have on public health policies in terms of what people may or may not be allowed to do. Finally, what type of medicine could be useful to combat the Coronavirus.

raw_comment: I've been hearing that the common flu is more dangerous than the new coronavirus, but looking at this graph, the coronavirus has a higher fatality rate and infection rate. This graph plots some of the most notorious infectious diseases on a plot of fatality rate vs infection rate, which is the average number of people infected by a sick person. raw_comment:
Headline: Chinese Response to Coronavirus Excessive?
     In this graph, I notice that the new coronavirus has a higher possible infectivity and higher amount of people infected by each sick person than some other serious diseases. It is deadlier than polio and more infectious than the common cold. However, it is less deadly than ebola, and smallpox and less infectious than measles and smallpox. I also notice that there is no set number for fatality rate or infection rate. Instead there is a red highlighted zone where it is thought to be. This shows how little data there still is on this virus. The fact that the zone of uncertainty places the death rate at anywhere from .1% to almost 5% and the infection rate from a little over 1 to almost 3 proves that more research should be done. 
         Due to the uncertainty about this virus, China has imposed a lockdown in Wuhan and surrounding areas to avoid spreading the virus. However, seeing that it is possible that the fatality rate is as low as .1% and that it is less deadly and infectious than most serious diseases makes me wonder if it is worth quarantining entire regions and restricting travel for millions. While there should still be quarantine for those confirmed infected and treatments should be a priority, perhaps the response, which had some adverse effects, like trapping vacationing foreigners in China, was too great. Hopefully, the spread of the coronavirus will soon be slowed and travel to China will be reopened.

raw_comment: One thing that I noticed in this graph was that most of the diseases that have a high fatality rate have some of the lowest numbers of people infected by one person. I also thought that it was interesting that someone with the seasonal flu will only infect one person, even though it often seems like the flu spreads very quickly. This makes me wonder what allows the diseases to spread so quickly if they typically only affect one to five people. Another thing that I noticed that I found surprising is that the seasonal flu has a higher fatality rate than polio.

raw_comment:
5th graders at Stedman Elementary in Denver, CO looked at this in Math Class today. 

We Noticed: 
- We think there's a box instead of a dot for the Corona Virus because it's new and scientists don't have as much data on it as the other diseases. 
- Smallpox seemed like the most dangerous, considering contagiousness and fatalities. 
- The graph is going up on the let side 10x each section. 
-All of the diseases seem to be airborne. 
-most of the diseases fall in-between 0 and 20% fatality rates.

We wondered: 
- Why are people so concerned about the Corona Virus when other diseases are as deadly or more deadly?
-Do newer diseases typically have more fatalities?
-What would this look like if it were organized by the year? 
-What years does this cover?
-How did researchers decide which viruses to include and which to leave out? 
- Is the chart based on the whole world? Are statistics the same everywhere?

raw_comment:
Severe Sicknesses

The first thing I saw in this graph was the large red box representing the coronavirus on the right side of the graph. Then, after taking a closer look, I saw the small yellow dots that represented several other diseases. I was surprised to see many diseases higher up on the scale of fatality rate than the coronavirus, but it is also a very new thing, so I'm sure it's just getting started. But I wonder, why is the coronavirus in a large red box instead of a small yellow dot like the rest? Perhaps it is because there is little known about the virus, but I'd be interested to have more information.
